questions.q: What does 'Acetylation' mean in Chapter 4?
options: A chemical modification that attaches a methyl group to a DNA base
A chemical modification that attaches ubiquitin to a histone
A chemical modification that attaches an acetyl group to a protein (histone)
A chemical modification that attaches a phosphate group to a protein
questions.why: Chapter 4 groups acetylation together with deacetylation and HDAC inhibitors: acetylation is a chemical mark on histones, and an HDAC inhibitor restores acetylation precisely by blocking deacetylation, reopening genes that had been silenced.

questions.q: In the context of Chapter 4, which class of therapeutic agent does 'Anti-PD-1 antibody' refer to?
options: A checkpoint inhibitor antibody that binds PD-1 on T cells and releases their brake
A cytotoxic drug that directly kills tumour cells
A methyltransferase that writes DNA methylation onto a promoter
questions.why: The book explains that an HDAC inhibitor induces PD-L1, creating 'gene addiction' and sensitising the tumour to checkpoint therapy; the agent that releases the PD-1 brake is exactly the anti-PD-1 antibody.

questions.q: In the biomarker studies of Chapter 4, which question does the AUC (area under the curve) answer?
options: Whether the sample size is large enough to support a statistical conclusion
How large the difference in a given marker is between different groups
How well a classifier (for example one using methylation to call a tumour) discriminates overall
questions.why: AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and the closer the value is to 1 the better the overall discriminating power of the classifier; the book uses the HCC classifier combining miR-15b and miR-130b with AUC = 0.981 as its example, and the case study question bank also reminds you that a cut-off still has to be set with ROC/AUC before clinical use.

questions.q: What is 'Bisulfite sequencing'?
options: A technique that cuts chromatin into 30 nm fibres
The gold standard method for detecting the methylation status of DNA
An assay that measures the degree of histone acetylation
A fluorescent test that resolves chromosome copy number
questions.why: The book states plainly that bisulfite sequencing is the gold standard: unmethylated C is converted to U while methylated C is retained, and that difference is what allows the positions of methylation to be read out.

questions.q: Which English term is the DNA sequence element on chromatin that marks a boundary and confines the range of action of an enhancer to a particular gene?
questions.why: A boundary element is the 'border' on chromatin: it delimits which genes an enhancer is allowed to influence and stops it acting across the boundary onto neighbouring genes. It is a DNA-sequence-level concept rather than a protein, so neither BRD4 nor Suv39h fits.

questions.q: What role does BRD4 play in Chapter 4?
options: A protein that reads histone acetylation marks with a bromodomain
A methyltransferase that writes DNA methylation
An ATP-dependent remodelling complex that slides nucleosomes along DNA
questions.why: Chapter 4 collects acetylation, deacetylation, HDAC inhibitors and BRD4 together: BRD4 recognises the acetylation mark through its bromodomain, so the amount of histone acetylation determines whether the chromatin is read and kept in an active state.

questions.q: What does 'CDKN2A' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: A gene responsible for establishing methylation marks de novo
A gene that maintains methylation marks after replication
A gene that repairs O6-methylguanine in glioma
A tumour suppressor gene that is silenced when its promoter is methylated
questions.why: The product of CDKN2A is p16; when its promoter is silenced by hypermethylation, one of the brakes on the cell cycle is removed. Among the methylation biomarkers he lists, the odds ratio for CDKN2A methylation/p16 loss is about 12.7 (p < 0.0001).

questions.q: Which English term denotes the free DNA fragments that circulate in blood and other body fluids and can be tracked by repeated blood sampling?
questions.why: cfDNA is the free DNA obtained from samples such as blood; it can be sampled repeatedly and interpreted through its methylation status, which is why Chapter 4 places it in the same biomarker context as AUC, confidence interval and odds ratio.

questions.q: What does 'Cellular memory' mean in Chapter 4?
options: The cell remembering chemical carcinogens it has once been exposed to
A memory effect of the cell membrane towards a particular drug
The ability of a cell to stably retain an epigenetic state
The immune memory produced by T cells after antigen stimulation
questions.why: DNA methylation and histone marks strengthen one another to form a positive-feedback loop, which lets the state maintain itself — this is cellular memory, and it keeps an already silenced gene silenced.

questions.q: Which English term is the family of chromatin remodelling proteins that carries a chromodomain and uses ATP to reposition nucleosomes?
questions.why: The name CHD comes from chromodomain (which recognises methylated histone marks) together with a DNA-binding region; like ISWI and INO80 it belongs to the ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling family and can slide nucleosomes along DNA.

questions.q: Which level of chromatin does 'Chromatin fibre' refer to?
options: The 2 nm level of the DNA double helix itself
The 1,400 nm chromosome that appears only during mitosis
Fibrous protein on the nuclear membrane
The 30 nm fibre formed when nucleosomes are strung together and coiled
questions.why: The packaging hierarchy runs DNA double helix 2 nm → nucleosome 11 nm → 30 nm chromatin fibre → 300 nm loop domain → 700 nm condensed region → 1,400 nm mitotic chromosome; the chromatin fibre is the level just above the nucleosome.

questions.q: How does a chromatin remodelling complex solve the problem of a 'promoter being covered by a nucleosome'?
options: Writing DNA methylation onto the promoter so that transcription factors cannot read it
Consuming ATP to slide or remove the nucleosome along the DNA, giving transcription factors and enhancers a chance to reach the promoter
Permanently excising histones from the chromatin
Cutting the chromatin fibre into 30 nm fragments
questions.why: Chapter 4 says that nucleosomes slide along the DNA to expose or cover a promoter, and one of the two forces driving that is the ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling complex; this kind of regulation is dynamic and reversible.

questions.q: What does 'CIMP' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: An abbreviation for a histone acetylation mark
A member of the chromatin remodelling complex family
The phenotype of widespread CpG island hypermethylation, associated with poor prognosis in colorectal cancer
Another name for the DNA repair enzyme MGMT
questions.why: CIMP stands for CpG island methylator phenotype; the quick-reference table records that in colorectal cancer it means widespread CpG island hypermethylation, with the clinical meaning of poor prognosis, and the odds ratio of CIMP-high versus CIMP-0 is 39.6 (95 % CI 20.6–76.1, p < 0.0001).

questions.q: When the book reports odds ratio 39.6, 95 % CI 20.6–76.1, p < 0.0001, that 20.6–76.1 is called the ______, meaning the range within which we can be 95 % confident the same effect estimate lies.
questions.why: A confidence interval is exactly this 'range of credibility'; the P-value answers 'could this be chance alone', the AUC measures the discriminating power of a classifier, and the odds ratio is the effect size itself.

questions.q: What does 'CpG island' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: A type of acetylation mark on a histone
A loop domain on the chromatin fibre
A stretch of DNA densely packed with CpG sites, usually located at a promoter
questions.why: A CpG island is a stretch of DNA in which CpG sites occur in dense clusters, and most lie at promoters; CIMP has to measure 'widespread CpG island hypermethylation' precisely because methylation in the promoter region switches a gene off.

questions.q: Which English term denotes the two adjacent bases on DNA in which a cytosine is followed by a guanine (5′-CG-3′)?
questions.why: A CpG site is a single pair of adjacent bases, whereas a CpG island is a stretch in which such sites occur in dense clusters. DNA methylation is written on the C base, so these two terms are the basic unit and the block of Chapter 4.

questions.q: What is the function of 'De novo methyltransferases'?
options: Copying existing marks onto the new strand after replication
Oxidising methylated cytosine back to the unmethylated state
Establishing brand-new methylation marks on previously unmethylated CpGs
Removing the acetyl group from histones
questions.why: The de novo methyltransferases are DNMT3A and DNMT3B, which establish marks from scratch; this and the maintenance of existing marks by DNMT1 are the most basic contrast, and they are the subject of the V12 clip.

questions.q: What does 'Deacetylation' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: Removing the acetyl group from histones
Reducing the number of turns of DNA wound around the nucleosome
questions.why: Deacetylation is what HDAC (histone deacetylase) does; once an HDAC inhibitor blocks it, histones become acetylated again and silenced genes are reactivated, and this is the main clinical thread running through Chapter 4.

questions.q: Which English term is the enzyme that reads the hemimethylated parent strand after DNA replication and copies the methylation mark onto the new strand?
questions.why: DNMT1 is the maintenance methyltransferase; by contrast, DNMT3A/DNMT3B are the de novo enzymes that establish new marks on previously unmethylated CpGs. Question (c) of Case 7 asks directly for the two classes of methyltransferase that maintain marks.

questions.q: Which English term is the pair of DNA methyltransferases that establish methylation marks from scratch on previously unmethylated CpGs?
questions.why: The quick-reference table writes the mechanism of epigenetic marks as 'DNMT3A/B establish, DNMT1 maintain'; the V12 clip likewise covers the de novo methyltransferase establishing new marks and the maintenance methyltransferase copying marks to the daughter strand.

questions.q: Germ cells are among the few cells in the body that erase existing DNA methylation marks and then rebuild them, which is also why the ______ becomes especially important here.
questions.why: Germ cells (during gametogenesis) erase and rebuild methylation marks, so the de novo methyltransferases that establish marks from scratch are especially important here; DNMT1's maintenance role is not the point.

questions.q: In the structure of the nucleosome, ______ is the linker histone: it binds the linker DNA between nucleosomes and is responsible for tightening the chromatin fibre.
questions.why: The quick-reference table gives the packaging hierarchy as '147 bp DNA wound around the H2A/H2B/H3/H4 octamer + H1'; H1 is the linker histone that tightens the thread, whereas the other three are names of histone modification marks.

questions.q: Broken down, the mark name H2A K119ub means: the lysine at position 119 of the ______ histone is ubiquitinated.
questions.why: The histone code is named as 'histone type + amino-acid position + type of modification': H2A K119ub means ubiquitin attached to lysine 119 of H2A, while H3K9me3 is trimethylation of lysine 9 of H3.

questions.q: H2B K123ub denotes which position on which histone?
questions.why: By the naming rules of the histone code, H2B K123ub means lysine 123 of H2B is ubiquitinated; it follows the same naming logic as H2A K119ub and H3 K79me.

questions.q: What does the histone mark 'H3 K4me' refer to?
options: Acetylation of lysine 4 on the H3 histone
Methylation of lysine 9 on the H3 histone
Methylation of lysine 4 on the H3 histone
Methylation of lysine 79 on the H3 histone
questions.why: A mark is named H (histone) + K (lysine) + position + type of modification; H3 K4me is methylation of lysine 4 of H3, while H3K4me3 is trimethylation of that same position and is associated with activation.

questions.q: What does 'H3 K79me' represent?
options: Methylation of lysine 79 of the H3 histone
Methylation of lysine 9 of the H3 histone
Methylation of lysine 4 of the H3 histone
Acetylation of lysine 79 of the H3 histone
questions.why: H3 K79me is methylation of lysine 79 of H3; in the same naming system H3K9me3 is a silencing mark and H3K4me3 an activation mark, and Chapter 4 makes the 'position' and the 'type of modification' of a mark must-distinguish items.

questions.q: Which category does the mark H3K4me3 fall into in Chapter 4?
options: A mark associated with gene silencing
A methyl mark found only on DNA
A mark associated with gene activation
questions.why: The book lists H3K9me3 as a silencing mark and H3K9ac as an activation mark; H3K4me3 is the activation mark of the promoter region and the opposite of the former, whereas methylation of a CpG island is the DNA-level silencing mechanism.

questions.q: What is the function of the histone mark H3K9me3?
options: Opening up chromatin so that transcription factors can reach the promoter
Recruiting HP1 to keep that region silent and compact
Adding acetyl groups to histones so that chromatin becomes active
Anchoring DNA methyltransferase onto the chromatin
questions.why: The quick-reference table states plainly H3K9me3 = silencing; it is a mark written by Suv39h, read out by HP1, and keeps that region in the silent state of heterochromatin.

questions.q: What does 'H4 K12ac' refer to?
options: Acetylation of lysine 8 of the H4 histone
Methylation of lysine 12 of the H4 histone
Acetylation of lysine 12 of the H4 histone
Acetylation of lysine 12 of the H3 histone
questions.why: H4 K12ac is the acetylation mark on lysine 12 of H4 and belongs to the same acetylation axis as H4 K8ac; acetylation loosens the chromatin so that it can be read.

questions.q: H4 K8ac and H4 K12ac are both ______ marks on the same histone: the acetyl group is added to lysine 8 and lysine 12, and they are associated with chromatin activation.
questions.why: ac stands for acetylation; in the same chapter H3K9me3 and H2A K119ub are methylation and ubiquitination respectively, while H4 K8ac and H4 K12ac belong to the acetylation family.

questions.q: What is the clinical significance of an HDAC inhibitor in Chapter 4?
options: Directly blocking DNA polymerase so that cancer cells cannot replicate
Permanently fixing the chromatin so that no gene can be expressed
Raising plasma fibrinogen so that the tumour embolises
Restoring histone acetylation and re-activating silenced genes, while inducing PD-L1 so that the tumour is sensitised to checkpoint therapy
questions.why: The quick-reference table records that an HDAC inhibitor restores histone acetylation, re-activates silenced genes and induces PD-L1, producing 'gene addiction' that sensitises the tumour to checkpoint therapy; he also lists it as an example of converting a cold tumour.

questions.q: What does 'Histone' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: An enzyme that cuts chromatin fibres
The collective term for the proteins around which DNA is wound to form the nucleosome
The telomere structure at the end of a chromosome
questions.why: Histones are what DNA is wound around: the nucleosome core is an octamer made of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, with H1 acting as the linker histone; their modifications make up the histone code of Chapter 4.

questions.q: Which English term is the recording rule by which 'the positions and types of modifications on histones jointly determine gene expression'?
questions.why: The histone code is the recording rule itself, for example H3K9me3 = histone 3, lysine at position 9, trimethylation; what actually executes that rule are the enzymes that write the marks (such as Suv39h) and the proteins that read them (such as HP1).

questions.q: This class of chemical change that adds an acetyl or methyl group to a histone and alters the chromatin state is collectively called a ______.
options: Histone variants (H2A, H2B, H3 and H4)
questions.why: A histone modification is the chemical change itself; the histone code is the naming system that decodes these marks into rules of gene expression, whereas histone variants are different versions of the protein that can be swapped in at the same position.

questions.term: Histone variants (H2A, H2B, H3 and H4)
questions.q: Which English term denotes the different versions of histones (H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 each having variants) that can occupy the same position, letting chromatin swap between different histones in different states?
options: Histone variants (H2A, H2B, H3 and H4)
questions.why: Histone variants are 'different versions at the same position', whereas a histone modification is 'a chemical modification on the same version'; the two are different concepts, and Chapter 4 lists the variants of all four core histones precisely to keep that layer clear.

questions.q: Which English term is the protein that recognises the silencing mark H3K9me3 and keeps that region in a silent state?
questions.why: HP1 is the reader: it recognises H3K9me3 and holds the region as silent, compact chromatin, whereas Suv39h is the enzyme that writes the mark — the reading and the writing on the same pathway.

questions.q: In the promoter region of a tumour suppressor gene, if the level of methylation is markedly higher than in normal tissue, that state is called ______.
questions.why: His account is that DNA methylation usually suppresses gene expression and that hypermethylation of a tumour suppressor promoter is a common driver of cancer; promoter hypermethylation therefore equals hypermethylated, which is putting the brake on hard.

questions.q: Different from having no methylation mark at all (unmethylated), the state in which the level of methylation is lower than in normal tissue but not entirely absent is called ______.
questions.why: Three terms must be kept apart: unmethylated means no methylation mark at all, hypomethylated means lower than normal but still present, and hypermethylated means higher than normal (promoter hypermethylation switches a gene off).

questions.q: What does 'IFN-γ' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: A member of the chromatin remodelling complex family
A cytokine signal secreted by immune cells that passes the signal into the nucleus via the STAT3 pathway
questions.why: Chapter 4 groups IFN-γ with STAT3: after the cytokine binds its receptor, STAT3 is phosphorylated and enters the nucleus, converting an extracellular signal into a change in gene expression.

questions.q: Within the ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling complex family, ______ uses ATP to pay for the energy that repositions nucleosomes along the DNA; ISWI and CHD are further examples in the same family.
questions.why: Chapter 4 says one of the two forces driving nucleosomes to slide along DNA is the ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling complex, and INO80, ISWI and CHD all belong to this family; BRD4, by contrast, is a protein that reads acetylation marks and is not on that list.

questions.q: Which English term is one of the ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling complex families, responsible for adjusting the spacing between nucleosomes and arranging chromatin more tightly or more loosely?
questions.why: ISWI is a member of the chromatin remodelling family, alongside INO80 and CHD, whose complexes consume ATP to reposition nucleosomes; BRD4 does not remodel chromatin — it reads acetylation marks with a bromodomain.

questions.q: Why is 'Lysine' important in Chapter 4?
options: The amino-acid side chain on histones that is acetylated, methylated or ubiquitinated
The base on DNA that is methylated
The ATP-binding subunit of the chromatin remodelling complex
The protein that links DNA between nucleosomes
questions.why: Almost every histone mark in Chapter 4 begins with K (H3K9me3, H4 K12ac, H2A K119ub and so on), and K stands for lysine; its side chain can carry a methyl, acetyl or ubiquitin group, which makes it the site of epigenetic marks.

questions.q: What is the function of 'Maintenance methyltransferases'?
options: Establishing brand-new marks on previously unmethylated CpGs
Removing the acetyl group from histones
Copying existing methylation marks onto the corresponding positions of the new strand after DNA replication
questions.why: The maintenance methyltransferase is DNMT1: after replication it reads the hemimethylated parent strand and copies the pattern onto the new strand; this is the other half of the distinction the V12 clip draws, the first half being the de novo methyltransferases that establish new marks.

questions.q: Which English term denotes the immune-suppressing cells of myeloid origin that damp down the anti-tumour immune response around a tumour?
questions.why: MDSCs are the suppressive cells of myeloid origin, belonging with Tregs and tumour-associated macrophages to the group that dampens immune attack around the tumour; an anti-PD-1 antibody, by contrast, is a therapeutic antibody used to release the T-cell brake.

questions.q: What does 'Methyl group' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: An acetyl group on a histone
A base pair of the DNA double helix
The small hydrocarbon group (CH₃) that is added to DNA and to histones
The core octamer of the nucleosome
questions.why: Methylation means adding a methyl group (CH₃): on DNA it is added to cytosine, and on histones this group is supplied by SAMe — it is the common raw material for both.

questions.q: What does 'Methylation' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: A chemical modification that adds a methyl group to DNA or histones and thereby regulates gene expression
Adding an acetyl group to histones
Removing the non-covalent forces between histones and DNA
Copying the parent strand's marks onto the new strand during DNA replication
questions.why: He says that DNA methylation is usually involved in the suppression of gene expression; the whole epigenetic machinery is staged on cytosine, because only cytosine gets methylated.

questions.q: What is the clinical significance of MGMT promoter methylation?
options: The widespread CpG island methylation of colorectal cancer, indicating poor prognosis
Loss of function of a chromatin remodelling complex, leaving the promoter unreadable
Increased histone acetylation, sensitising the tumour to HDAC inhibitors
In glioma the DNA repair enzyme is silenced, so patients are more sensitive to alkylating chemotherapy plus radiotherapy and in fact have a better prognosis
questions.why: Case 7: MGMT promoter methylation → MGMT is silenced → O6-methylguanine lesions cannot be repaired → greater sensitivity to alkylating agents such as temozolomide and to radiotherapy, with a better prognosis; this is the standard example of a methylation biomarker.

questions.q: What is 'Multivariate logistic regression'?
options: A test comparing the survival curves of different groups
A statistical method that puts several variables into one model at the same time to estimate the probability of an event
A classifier that splits samples into two groups and finds the best cut-off
Resolving DNA methylation sites by making crystal structures of them
questions.why: It is part of the biomarker statistics in Chapter 4: when several variables (for example several methylation sites plus clinical variables) have to be considered together to predict a patient's outcome, this is used to build the model, and the results are reported alongside the AUC and the odds ratio.

questions.q: The binding of histone to DNA is ______ (hydrogen bonds plus electrostatic attraction), which is why the chromatin state can change dynamically and reversibly.
questions.why: Chapter 4 points out that the binding of histone to DNA is non-covalent and therefore can change at any time; Acetylation, Deacetylation and Methylation are all chemical modifications acting on histones, not ways of binding.

questions.q: Which English term denotes the assembly of eight histone molecules, two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, that forms the nucleosome core?
questions.why: The core is the octamer, two copies of each core histone; H1 is a separate linker histone that is not part of the core octamer, so the nucleosome is 147 bp of DNA wound around the octamer plus H1.

questions.q: What does 'Odds ratio' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: The sensitivity of a given test
The mean difference in a given marker between different samples
The ratio of the odds of an event in two groups, used to quantify the association between methylation and disease or treatment response
questions.why: The numbers he gives are exactly this use: when methylation is detected the odds ratio is about 12.7, and the odds ratio of CIMP-high versus CIMP-0 is 39.6 (95 % CI 20.6–76.1, p < 0.0001).

questions.q: When a single signalling pathway corresponds one-to-one in both Drosophila and humans, that cross-species conserved correspondence is called ______; it is precisely the premise on which model organisms can be used to study human disease.
questions.why: In lecture one he lists orthology (a pathway conserved across species) as a key learning point: because histones are highly conserved between species, the Drosophila-to-human correspondence holds and results from model organisms can be extrapolated to humans.

questions.q: What does 'P-value' refer to in Chapter 4?
options: The credible range of an estimate
The probability of obtaining the current or a more extreme result under the null hypothesis, used to judge whether the result could be chance alone
The overall discriminating power of a classifier
questions.why: Every statistical conclusion in the book carries a p value (the CIMP comparison p < 0.0001, CDKN2A methylation p < 0.0001); the p value answers 'could this be chance alone', not how large the effect is — that comes from the odds ratio.

questions.q: Which English term is the cell-cycle inhibitor protein encoded by the CDKN2A gene?
questions.why: p16 is the product of CDKN2A; when the CDKN2A promoter is silenced by methylation, p16 is lost and one of the brakes on the cell cycle is removed — it is also one of the methylation biomarkers he lists.

questions.q: What does the positive-feedback loop between DNA methylation and histone marks explain?
options: Chromatin stops changing once the remodelling complexes run out of ATP
Methyltransferase evenly divides the marks between the two new strands at replication
An HDAC inhibitor swaps the direction of acetylation and methylation
The two strengthen one another so that an established or silenced state can maintain itself — that is, cellular memory
questions.why: The book describes this cross-talk as DNA methylation and histone marks strengthening one another to form a positive-feedback loop → cellular memory; this is exactly the mechanism by which an epigenetic state can be 'remembered'.

questions.q: What is the role of 'S-adenosyl methionine (SAMe)' in Chapter 4?
options: The raw material for histone acetylation
The supplier that donates the methyl group when DNA and histones are methylated
An alternative energy source to ATP for the chromatin remodelling complex
A sequence used as a template during DNA repair
questions.why: The methyl groups for both DNA and histone methylation are donated by SAMe, the universal methyl donor; without it DNMT could not write a methyl onto cytosine.

questions.q: Which English term is the reagent used to treat DNA in bisulfite sequencing that converts unmethylated cytosine to uracil?
questions.why: Sodium bisulfite changes only unmethylated C (into U) and leaves methylated C intact; it is this difference that allows the positions of methylation to be read out, which is why bisulfite sequencing is the gold standard.

questions.q: Which English term is the signal-transducing protein that carries a cytokine signal (such as IFN-γ) all the way to the nucleus, where it regulates gene expression?
questions.why: STAT3 is the signal-transducing protein: after the cytokine binds its receptor it is phosphorylated and enters the nucleus, converting an extracellular signal into a change in gene expression; BRD4, HP1 and TET are all chromatin-level proteins.

questions.q: Which English term is the methyltransferase responsible for writing the silencing mark H3K9me3 onto histones?
questions.why: Suv39h is the enzyme that writes the mark, whereas HP1 is the protein that reads H3K9me3 and maintains silencing; TET and DNMT1 act at the DNA level, not on histones.

questions.q: What role do enzymes such as TET play in DNA methylation?
options: Writing methyl groups onto previously unmethylated CpGs
Oxidising methylated cytosine (for example 5mC → 5hmC), taking part in demethylation
Reading the hemimethylated parent strand and maintaining the mark
questions.why: The TET family are the enzymes of the DNA demethylation pathway, oxidising 5mC to intermediates such as 5hmC and ultimately removing the methyl mark; they run in the opposite direction to DNMT3A/DNMT3B, which establish marks, and DNMT1, which maintains them.

questions.q: What is the context of 'TMZ' (temozolomide) in Chapter 4?
options: An inhibitor of the histone deacetylase enzymes
An alkylating drug that adds a methyl group at the O6 position of guanine, directly relevant to interpreting prognosis from MGMT promoter methylation
An inhibitor of the chromatin remodelling complex
questions.why: Case 7: in glioma patients whose MGMT promoter is methylated, MGMT is silenced and O6-methylguanine lesions cannot be repaired, so they are more sensitive to temozolomide combined with radiotherapy and in fact have a better prognosis.

questions.q: Why is 'Tumor suppressor' particularly important in Chapter 4?
options: If their promoters are silenced by hypermethylation, that is like removing the brake, and they become a driver of cancer
They lose function only through gene mutation
Their function is to promote cell division
They are expressed only in immune cells
questions.why: He points out that DNA methylation usually suppresses gene expression and that hypermethylation of a tumour suppressor promoter is a common driver of cancer — that is putting the brake on hard, and CDKN2A and p16 are the examples.

questions.q: In bisulfite sequencing, a cytosine with no methylation mark at all is converted to U; this completely unmethylated state is called ______.
questions.why: Bisulfite changes only unmethylated C (into U) and leaves methylated C intact; so the positions that read out as U are the unmethylated sites — which is why bisulfite sequencing can serve as the gold standard.
